rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, 3-year field factorial experiment at Citra FL with own measurements of irrigation, drainage, leaching, plant N. Q2: Table 1 reports irrigation applied (e.g. 2006: SUR 186 mm, SDI 275 mm vs TIME 391 mm); Abstract and Sec. 3.2/Fig. 3/Table 5 report SMS-based SUR and SDI reduced percolated volume and NO3-N leaching by about 90% vs TIME. Q3: Abstract and Sec. 3.2 state leaching/fertilizer displacement under TIME was detected both by EC/soil-moisture capacitance probes (Figs. 5-6) and by drainage lysimeters (Figs. 3-4, Table 5). Q4: Sec. 3.2 and Fig. 6 show soil moisture spikes above field capacity at 0.37 and 0.67 m under TIME and none under SMS, described as the mechanistic driving force behind the leaching differences; EC patterns show fertilizer displacement below root zone. Q8: Sec. 3.2 notes EC measurements were not ion specific so other ions may have influenced readings; Sec. 2 notes the twin-line (separate irrigation/fertigation) setup was for experimental convenience and differs from commercial practice. Q9: Figs. 3 and 4 give error bars as standard error of the mean (n=4) for leachate volume and NO3-N leaching.
rows.notes: Single sandy soil, single site, single crop, plot-scale trial; detailed irrigation water savings percentages are mostly reported in the companion paper (Zotarelli et al. 2009) but Table 1 here reports applied irrigation volumes. Q7 judged no: statements that high-frequency low-volume irrigation suits low water-holding sandy soils and 'appropriate use' are not framed as stated requirements. Irrigation volume savings themselves have no dispersion measure; SE applies to leaching/percolation results.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, 3-year field experiment with own harvest data. Q2: Table 3 and Sec. 3.1 report fruit dry biomass for SMS-based SUR and SDI was on average 37%, 17% and 16% higher than TIME in 2005, 2006 and 2007, with shoot dry weight also generally higher. Q4: Sec. 3.1, Table 4 and Fig. 2 measure plant N accumulation, daily N uptake rate and petiole sap NO3, and the authors link lower uptake under TIME to excessive leaching hampering canopy development and yield. Q8: Sec. 2 notes the twin drip-line setup was for experimental convenience and a commercial grower would use one line; Sec. 3.1 notes 2005 hot/wet conditions and bacterial spot lowered yields. Q9: Table 2 reports CV% for shoot and fruit dry biomass; Fig. 2 reports standard errors (n=4) for N accumulation.
rows.notes: Yield effect here is fruit dry biomass; fresh marketable yield increases (11-26%) are reported in the companion paper and only cited. Yield measured by a single method (harvest), so no triangulation. Single soil/crop/site, plot scale. Q9 is a weak yes: only an ANOVA CV% is given for biomass, no per-treatment SD/SE.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a primary 3-year plot trial on one sandy soil (Candler sand) with one tomato cultivar; soil moisture sensor-based irrigation (capacitance ECH2O probes with QIC controller) is the technology tested against fixed-time irrigation.
